body_html:
Talking about feelings in Spanish takes more than a vocabulary list. Spanish expresses emotions through several structures, estar, sentirse, tener and verbs like dar and poner, and each one feels slightly different. Once you know them, you can say not just “I’m sad” but “it makes me sad”, “I’m afraid” or “it gets on my nerves” the way native speakers do.

Key takeaways
  • Use estar or sentirse for how you feel right now.
  • Some emotions use tener: tengo miedo, tengo vergüenza.
  • Me da… and me pone… describe what causes a feeling.
  • Regional words matter: enojado (Latin America) vs enfadado (Spain).
{{toc}}

Talking about feelings in Spanish with estar and sentirse

For emotional states, use estar (to be) or sentirse (to feel). Both are natural; sentirse is slightly more personal.

  • Estoy contento / contenta. I’m happy.
  • Me siento triste. I feel sad.
  • Estoy nervioso / nerviosa. I’m nervous.
  • Me siento solo / sola. I feel lonely.

Why estar and not ser? Because feelings are states, not identity. Estoy aburrido means “I’m bored”; soy aburrido means “I’m boring”. I explain the difference in {{link:ser-vs-estar|ser vs estar}}.

Ilusionado deserves a special mention. It describes the hopeful excitement of looking forward to something, from a trip to a new relationship, and the noun ilusión carries the same warmth. The RAE dictionary lists this sense alongside the “illusion” meaning learners expect.

{{image:2}}

Feelings with tener

Some emotions are things you “have” in Spanish:

  • Tengo miedo. I’m afraid.
  • Tengo vergüenza. I’m embarrassed / ashamed.
  • Tengo celos. I’m jealous.
  • Tengo ganas de verte. I want to see you / I’m looking forward to seeing you.

Me da… and me pone…: what causes a feeling

To say that something causes an emotion, Spanish often uses dar or poner with an indirect object, like gustar:

  • Me da miedo manejar de noche. Driving at night scares me.
  • Me da pena. It embarrasses me / I feel bad (much of Latin America); It makes me sad (Spain).
  • Me da rabia. It makes me furious.
  • Me pone nervioso hablar en público. Speaking in public makes me nervous.
  • Me pone de mal humor. It puts me in a bad mood.

Notice me da pena: its meaning shifts by region, a perfect example of why emotional language is hard to translate.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Becoming: getting angry, sad or nervous

To describe a change of emotion, Spanish uses ponerse: Me puse nervioso (I got nervous), Se puso triste (She became sad). Many emotion verbs are also reflexive: enojarse / enfadarse (to get angry), alegrarse (to be glad), preocuparse (to worry). For more on “becoming”, see {{link:ponerse-volverse-hacerse|ponerse, volverse, hacerse}}.

Positive feelings worth knowing

  • Estoy orgulloso / orgullosa de ti. I’m proud of you.
  • Me siento agradecido / agradecida. I feel grateful.
  • ¡Qué alivio! Estoy aliviado. What a relief! I’m relieved.
  • Estoy enamorado / enamorada. I’m in love.
  • Me hace muy feliz. It makes me very happy.
  • Me alegra mucho verte. I’m so glad to see you.

Making feelings stronger or softer

Intensity matters as much as the emotion itself. Spanish speakers adjust it with small words:

SofterNeutralStronger
un poco triste (a bit sad)tristemuy triste, tristísimo (very sad)
algo nervioso (somewhat nervous)nerviososúper nervioso (super nervous, informal)
más o menos (so-so)biengenial, fenomenal (great)
regular (not great)malfatal (awful, Spain)

The suffix -ísimo is especially expressive: contentísima, cansadísimo. And when someone asks ¿Qué tal?, answering regular is an honest, culturally normal way to say you are not having a great day.

Asking someone how they feel

  • ¿Cómo te sientes? How do you feel?
  • ¿Cómo estás, de verdad? How are you, really?
  • ¿Qué te pasa? What’s wrong?
  • ¿Te molestó lo que dije? Did what I said bother you?
{{image:3}}

A sample conversation

  • A: ¿Cómo estás, de verdad? (How are you, really?)
  • B: Un poco agobiada. Tengo mucho trabajo y me da miedo no llegar a tiempo. (A bit overwhelmed. I have a lot of work and I’m scared I won’t make it in time.)
  • A: Te entiendo. A mí también me pone nerviosa tener plazos tan cortos. (I understand. Short deadlines make me nervous too.)
  • B: Pero estoy ilusionada con el proyecto. (But I’m excited about the project.)

One last tip: Spanish speakers often answer ¿Cómo estás? with more honesty than you might expect. Saying Pues, la verdad, un poco cansado (Well, honestly, a bit tired) is not oversharing; it is simply normal conversation, and it invites the other person to share too.

Common mistakes

  • Estoy excitado for “I’m excited”. Use emocionado or ilusionado.
  • Estoy embarazada for “I’m embarrassed”. It means pregnant.
  • Soy triste. Use estoy triste for a feeling.
  • Siento triste. The verb is reflexive: me siento triste.

Being able to name feelings makes every relationship easier, from {{link:how-to-comfort-someone-in-spanish|comforting a friend}} to everyday conversations. For more real-life situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

Final thoughts

Talking about feelings in Spanish opens a deeper kind of conversation. Learn the four patterns (estar, sentirse, tener and me da / me pone) and you will be able to say what is really going on inside, not just that you are “fine”.

faq.q: How do you say “I feel” in Spanish?
faq.a: Use the reflexive verb sentirse: me siento feliz (I feel happy), me siento cansado (I feel tired).

faq.q: What does me da pena mean?
faq.a: In Spain it usually means “it makes me sad” or “what a pity”. In much of Latin America it often means “it embarrasses me”.

faq.q: What is the difference between enojado and enfadado?
faq.a: Both mean angry. Enojado is more common in Latin America and enfadado in Spain.
